title: Behind the lens with Mark Sutton for Antonelli's F1 title triumph
excerpt:
'One of the best experiences of my life' – Mark Sutton on photographing Antonelli's F1 title

From photographing Ayrton Senna to capturing a young Kimi Antonelli meeting Lewis Hamilton, Mark Sutton reflects on four decades documenting Formula 1 and why this season has been one of his most memorable.

Nov 15, 2026 5:06pm UTC

After more than four decades photographing Formula 1's biggest names and most memorable moments, Mark Sutton thought he had seen it all. But Kimi Antonelli's remarkable 2026 season has given the veteran photographer a renewed enthusiasm for his craft.

From capturing a young Antonelli meeting Lewis Hamilton to documenting the Italian's maiden World Championship triumph, Sutton has witnessed some extraordinary moments. Yet it was Antonelli's emotional home victory at Monza that provided one of the highlights of his career.

"That was one of the most incredible experiences of my life," he recalls of Kimi Antonelli's emotional home victory at Monza.

"We posed Kimi up, and there was this sea of people in front of him: 10, 20, 30,000, I don't know how many there were on the circuit.

"It's an experience like nothing else in Formula 1."

It was one of many moments Sutton captured during the Italian's second Formula 1 season, which culminated in a maiden Drivers' Championship in Mexico City and helped Mercedes secure the Constructors' title in Brazil. For Sutton, the experience has also rekindled his enthusiasm for the job.

"All the photographers talk about how amazing he is. It has really kept me going this year because, when you get to 61, the job can become a little repetitive: not boring, but repetitive.

It's great to have a fresh perspective on things and a bit of new life. It's really woken me up. It's been a joy, to be honest, absolutely amazing."

Photographing legends in the making

Sutton's first experience behind a camera at a race came in 1983, when his brother Keith, then working as Ayrton Senna's photographer, invited him to Oulton Park. Sutton was 18, still studying and unfamiliar with the equipment.

"He said, 'I'm going to do the first corner. You go out the back.' I had a camera with no motor drive, so I had to take a picture and then wind the film on manually."

The race featured Senna battling Martin Brundle in British Formula 3, and Sutton suddenly found himself watching a dramatic incident unfold through his lens.

"Senna dived down the inside of Martin Brundle... and the next minute they landed on top of each other. But I didn't get the next frame because I had to wind the film on. By the time I'd done that, it was gone. I did get pictures of them walking around the car afterwards. Those photographs from my first ever race became quite famous."

The photographs became well-known images of Senna's early career, as the Brazilian went on to claim that year's British F3 title before progressing to Formula 1, where he would win three World Championships. Sutton, meanwhile, photographed Senna's first Toleman test and built a career documenting generations of drivers.

"And that was photographing Senna, when nobody really knew what a legend he was going to become," Sutton reflects.

More than three decades later, Sutton would capture another photograph involving a future World Champion, although once again, its significance wouldn't become clear until years afterwards.

At the 2018 Italian Grand Prix, a 12-year-old Antonelli was taking part in the pre-race ceremonies as a grid kid. As the drivers made their way along the line, Sutton was photographing their interactions with the children.

Among those moments was a young Antonelli fist-bumping Lewis Hamilton, then driving for Mercedes.

"My photograph was the one of Kimi with Lewis back in 2018," Sutton reveals.

"Little did I know what that photograph would become. It's crazy, isn't it? Kimi was a grid kid at Monza in 2018. I was photographing the drivers going down the line, high-fiving and fist-bumping the kids. One of those moments was Lewis fist-bumping a 12-year-old Kimi."

Eight years later, the boy in that photograph has succeeded Hamilton at Mercedes and become a World Champion himself.

A sea of Tifosi and a moment in history

Of all the events Sutton photographed in 2026, Antonelli's home victory at Monza stands apart. With thousands of Tifosi flooding the circuit to celebrate their home hero, Sutton found himself on the podium capturing what would become one of the most memorable moments of his career.

"I felt this massive buzz. I turned around afterwards and said to everybody, 'That was one of the best experiences of my life.'

"I think that's what doing this job is about as well, having that chance to experience these things. What other job allows you to travel around the world and take pictures?"

Having attended races with his father since he was just two years old and more than four decades photographing motorsport, Sutton has experienced countless memorable moments, but few atmospheres compare to Monza and the passion of the Italian fans.

"The key thing is the fans. You've got fans in the grandstands, fans on the track, and people down in the pit lane and on the pit wall. It's like a threefold effect. The noise is amazing, and the Italian fans are just incredible."

One image in particular has stayed with him – Antonelli, an Italian flag across his shoulders, standing before the enormous crowd of the Tifosi. Sutton watched as the driver briefly lowered his head, seemingly taking in the scale of the occasion.

Kimi Antonelli of Italy and Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team celebrates on the podium with his trophy during the F1 Grand Prix of Italy at Autodromo Nazionale Monza on September 06, 2026 in Monza, Italy. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Kimi Antonelli with Simone Resta, Deputy Technical Director of Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team during the F1 Grand Prix of Italy at Autodromo Nazionale Monza on September 06, 2026 in Monza, Italy. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Kimi Antonelli on the podium with his trophy during the F1 Grand Prix of Italy at Autodromo Nazionale Monza on September 06, 2026 in Monza, Italy. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Kimi Antonelli drinks Champagne on the podium during the F1 Grand Prix of Italy at Autodromo Nazionale Monza on September 06, 2026 in Monza, Italy. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

"I felt that it was a really important photograph.

"I started shouting to get him to look up. Then he raised his fist and looked directly at me. That was a great picture."

The opportunities continued as Antonelli returned to pose with members of his inner circle.

"I was very lucky because Kimi posed for us, and then he wanted another picture. He came back with his trainer and wanted a picture with him. Then he came back with his engineer, so we carried on taking these photographs."

Sutton later found an elevated position to photograph Mercedes' team celebrations below, while colleagues covered the pit wall, crowd and podium from other angles. Antonelli even removed his shirt and threw it towards the fans, prolonging the celebrations.

"That was probably the most important photo shoot of the season," Sutton says. "I think Getty Images absolutely smashed it. We got every angle possible."

The photographs meant something to the team, too. Weeks later, Mercedes asked Sutton about obtaining the picture of Antonelli with his trainer.

"It's an iconic podium, and it's a privilege to be there photographing somebody who would go on to become World Champion."

Capturing a World Champion in Mexico City

Mexico City brought a different challenge. Antonelli clinched the championship with a podium finish, and Sutton was among the photographers documenting the celebrations that followed.

"The one in Mexico was particularly chaotic. We call it a 'bunfight' because it's literally elbows out," he recalls.

"First, we photographed the team, but his dad and family weren't there, so we had to do it again. Then [Mercedes’ Content Director] Paul Ripke said we'd got all the champagne ready, but there were certain pictures he wanted us to get first.

"All of a sudden, the champagne was handed out and everything went crazy."

The excitement made even an experienced photographer reconsider his position.

"One mechanic lifted Kimi up, but he couldn't see because Kimi was pouring champagne over his face. He was almost walking around blindfolded. It was hilarious. I felt I was too close. I was shooting on a wide lens, a 14-24mm, but I was almost right up his nose. Sometimes you want to be a little farther back."

But Sutton's photographs also captured smaller encounters during the weekend. He watched Antonelli walk along both lines of grid kids, greeting them individually, and photographed a young karter named Emma Garcia Lopez giving him a bracelet, which the Italian was later seen wearing on the podium during his championship celebrations.

"She then shared the story, but she didn't have my photograph, so I completed the story for her with that picture," he explains.

"Knowing that those children in Mexico have interacted with a World Champion is special. It gives them a memento of the race, and maybe a bit of encouragement."

A different side of the champion in Brazil

By the time Formula 1 arrived in Sao Paulo, Antonelli was already champion, while Mercedes would go on to secure the Constructors' Championship. Sutton's most memorable encounters there, however, came away from the racing.

On Thursday, Antonelli surprised him with a fist bump as he arrived at the circuit.

"I'd followed him coming in, and suddenly he put his fist right into my lens," Sutton laughs. "Sometimes you ask drivers to do it, and they will, but with Kimi it felt like a little bit of respect."

The interaction also highlights the mutual appreciation between Antonelli and those documenting his career, something Sutton believes the young champion has understood despite being only in his second F1 season.

"He knows my name. I think generally he'll know all the photographers' names," Sutton says. "He's a clever guy, and he understands that the media is part of this circus and that he has to get them on his side."

Sutton later found himself alone in the pit lane as Antonelli visited the Mercedes mechanics, waved a Brazilian flag and then leaned over to kiss the halo of his car.

"When you're photographing a car on track, you can't really see the driver. You can only see the helmet. Of course, there's a lot of skill involved, and we take some beautiful, amazing photographs. But for me, it's sometimes more about the face: the reactions, the smiles."

He sees echoes of Senna in Antonelli's willingness to joke around with his team, particularly in his playful relationship with race engineer Peter 'Bono' Bonnington. Sutton remembers Senna's prank-filled friendship with Gerhard Berger, although he is careful not to equate the two drivers.

"I think they're different characters, but there are similarities," he says. "I didn't know Senna particularly well, but I think he was quite a joker in the paddock, especially with the teams. I think having that relaxed side is important, rather than being too serious all the time."

A frame of history

Some of Sutton's most significant photographs have taken on new meaning over the years. His early images of Senna and the 2018 photograph of Hamilton meeting a young Antonelli show how moments captured almost by chance can become an important part of Formula 1 history.

"Sometimes that's just how this job works. You're in the right place, with the right lens, the right exposure and the right light."

These fleeting moments, Sutton believes, demonstrate photography's unique ability to preserve the stories and emotions that define the sport.

"I think what it is with photographers is that we capture a particular moment in history. It's frozen. It's not video coverage, where you're filming a particular sequence. We're capturing a sequence as well, but we'll generally use that one particular frame.

"And that one frame can be a magical moment."

Getty Images is now assembling a dedicated collection of Antonelli photographs from the season. Sutton hopes the images will capture not only the trophies and champagne, but also the expressions and interactions that made this championship distinctive.

With three races still remaining, he is looking forward to seeing what else his camera might capture. Yet his memory of Monza is already secure.

"Monza was magical, absolutely magical," he says.

"Kimi has given me a boost, if anything. I'm looking forward to next year now, but I'm also looking forward to the last three races and finishing this season. It's been incredible."

title: Button explains what will ‘keep Alonso going’ at Aston Martin
excerpt:
Jenson Button believes that Fernando Alonso’s re-signing with Aston Martin is hugely important for the team and, as long as he can see progress, that will “keep him going”.

At the end of September it was confirmed that 45-year-old Alonso would be continuing at Aston Martin, with the squad running an unchanged line-up of the Spaniard and Lance Stroll for 2027.

That latest deal will see the two-time World Champion – who won his titles two decades ago with Renault – compete in his 24th F1 season next year as the Silverstone-based outfit look to bounce back from a challenging 2026.

The team currently sit 10th in the Constructors’ Championship and required a B-spec update in Hungary to lift their performance level. However, even with that positive step, their engine supplier Honda have been off in terms of performance while reliability has also been a struggle.

However, Aston Martin still hold lofty ambitions for the future having also brought in the likes of Team Principal Adrian Newey in a bid to reach the top, and for 2009 F1 World Champion Jenson Button – an Aston Martin Ambassador – seeing signs of progress will be crucial in keeping Alonso involved with the project.

“I mean, there always has to be a little bit of doubt, because he's 45 years old now,” Button told F1.com when asked if there were any doubts Alonso would stick around. “I've been out of the sport for 10 years, and I retired because I was tired!

“I mean it always has to be a little bit of that, but it amazes me – his dedication and how much he loves competing at the top level, and he's still got it. So why not then keep going until he doesn't want it anymore?

“He is going to want to see progress, that is the main thing. He probably knows he's not going to win races any time soon, but as long as he can see progress and he is moving closer to that win, that’s what’s going to keep him going.”

Alonso credits 'phenomenal' car after strong drive in Brazil

‘I don’t know how he does it’

With Alonso and Aston Martin preparing for a fifth campaign together next year, it’s the latest chapter in a remarkable F1 career that began in 2001 with Minardi. Since then, he has gone on to represent the likes of Renault, McLaren and Ferrari while continuously operating at an elite level, with the Spaniard turning 46 midway through next season.

“I don't know how he does it,” Button continued. “I really don't. He lives racing, he lives F1. When he's not in an F1 car he's in a go-kart on his track or he's driving ex-DTM cars.

“He's always driving something, and that's his passion, and he likes driving on dirt as well. He keeps himself very busy with racing, and fair play to him.

“For me, it was great to retire from F1 to go and do other things. Also, I’ve got other things I want to do in life, but his dedication to motorsport is undeniable and I think unparallelled.”

When asked if he’s still operating at his best-ever level, Button responded: “I don’t think you can compare really because the sport’s changed so much. But he’s still putting in an unbelievable effort and also what he's achieving.

“It's funny with Fernando, because most drivers look very similar. If you put them all in the same kind of car, you wouldn't be able to tell who's who.

“With Fernando you tell immediately. He's up in the steering wheel and he's [doing these] little adjustments the whole time and it's great to have the talent of Fernando in the sport.”

‘It seems to work really well’

Alonso’s partnership with Aston Martin has often felt like an ideal match, particularly in 2023 when he scored eight podiums on his way to a P4 finish in the Drivers’ Championship. Even this year, given the struggles the team have faced, the fact the Spaniard has still amassed seven points is a credit to his never-ending determination.

For Button that’s also how it has felt, as he highlighted the importance of a team’s atmosphere in helping drivers excel.

“A few years ago, when they were getting podiums, it felt amazing,” Button recalled. “But now I think someone with his experience, this team has had world champions racing for them for quite a few years now, and I think it's an interesting brand for racing drivers.

“We love cars, it's got Aston Martin in the title – that’s nice – but to be fair it's more about the performance on track and the team of people you have around you. You need them to believe in you as well, and sometimes that doesn't happen with a team, and you see it time and time again with drivers jumping in cars.

“You know, they're the next big thing and then it doesn't work. You go somewhere else and then it works, so atmosphere is really important in making sure drivers feel comfortable and they can maximise their talents and skills. It seems to work really well, and [Alonso] seems at home.”

For that reason, when it was confirmed that Alonso would be sticking around with the team into next season, it served as an important boost for everyone involved in the project.

“I think that's really important for this team and continuity with both drivers is really important,” Button said, commenting on that announcement. “They've been through the rough and hoping for the smooth, and the feedback from both of them is really key.

“Fernando is obviously the one that's won the world championships, but Lance's feedback is also important. We need two drivers' feedback to enhance the car and [to make] a car that works for both drivers as well, you need that. That's when you're fighting for points.”

title: Our writers on Antonelli’s title success and what it means
excerpt:
It’s been a couple of weeks since Kimi Antonelli became the youngest World Champion in Formula 1 history, so now feels like a perfect time to reflect on exactly what his success means for both him and the sport.

We asked our writers Lawrence Barretto, Chris Medland and James Hinchcliffe to give us their thoughts on his record-breaking title…

Lawrence Barretto (F1 Correspondent & Presenter)

I first spent some proper time with Antonelli back in 2024 at Monza. It came just a day after he crashed on his FP1 debut but you wouldn't have known it. He'd already addressed it, learned from it and compartmentalised it. Admittedly, Mercedes had also just announced he would get his F1 debut the following year with the team, but the way he was handling everything was impressive.

He needed all that mental strength in his rookie year as he encountered a rollercoaster season that yielded some brilliant highs – such as three podiums – but also some painful lows, including scoring just one point across the entire European leg that culminated in boss Toto Wolff calling his performance at his home race in Monza "underwhelming".

Once again, Antonelli didn't let anything get him down. His close-knit family unit and inner circle of Mercedes team members whom he had bonded with since he joined the programme provided him with the bubble he needed to avoid spiraling, reset and go again in search of the immense potential they were convinced he had.

So, when Mercedes offered him a title-contending car for 2026, a year earlier than they had planned – and after a winter where he knuckled down and learned all the harsh lessons he'd been handed in 2025 – Antonelli seized his opportunity and never looked back.

As his more experienced team mate and title favourite George Russell toiled, Antonelli excelled. It's true that Antonelli didn't know what he didn't know regarding the enormity of fighting for the F1 title but all the evidence from the last two years proved he was made of special stuff – and it's still on him to deliver.

Nine Grand Prix wins, including stunning victories in Monza and Austin, showed just how good he is in just his second season. To win a title so quickly, and take the mantle from four-time World Champion Sebastian Vettel as the youngest ever champion, was remarkable. And he's not changed one bit from the charming, funny, kind and thoughtful guy I chatted to back in 2024.

Chris Medland (Special Contributor)

I don’t mind admitting I made some pretty poor predictions ahead of the 2026 season, but I definitely didn’t feel like I was being overly harsh on Kimi expecting a season of highs and lows. I had him down for a few wins and some real flashes of brilliance, but a lack of consistency up against Russell, who I thought would win the title.

It’s easy to point to the new generation of car as levelling the playing field, and in many ways it did as Russell had three years of ground effect experience when Antonelli made his debut, but Russell had also raced the previous generation of car and had adapted well already. For Antonelli to be so much stronger than his team mate this year should not be dismissed as just down to the regulations.

The step forward has been remarkable, but I think what really stands out is the way in which Antonelli has handled pressure. It barely seemed to affect him at any stage. He maximised his race result so often, and that did not drop even as he took the title. He said he was tense in Mexico City but the only time he wasn’t on it in the race was the final lap when he had to back off due to tears.

The records Antonelli has broken on his way to maiden title

He even erred on the more cautious side in wheel-to-wheel battles at first (think back to the Sprint in Canada) and then pushed the limits slightly more once he knew where the line was in the internal battle at Mercedes. He’s also raced others really well, too, taking a patient approach.

Antonelli was so good this year that he actually was rarely tested in terms of a high-pressure title battle or that many intense on-track fights, but the prospect of seeing him in both in future is exciting. He has so much developing still to do, and so much potential, that this genuinely feels like the beginning of a special career.

His race engineer Peter Bonnington said Antonelli can definitely match the likes of Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher given his ability. That’s huge praise, but also depends on him being given another title-contending car next year. I really hope he gets it, because the idea of him fighting Hamilton, Max Verstappen and even Lando Norris – three other champions in three different teams – in 2027 is mouthwatering.

James Hinchcliffe (IndyCar Race Winner and Analyst)

With Antonelli’s podium in Mexico City, which he shared with Verstappen and Hamilton, we saw another record fall to the Italian. One that, barring some nearly unimaginable miracle, may never be beaten. Taking the crown of youngest World Champion from Vettel by over three years is a truly monumental feat. It’s the type of statistic that usually leads a list of career accomplishments that most could only dream of.

It really does feel like just the start for Antonelli. This did not feel like a flash in the pan type of performance. This wasn’t a ‘lucky’ year where everything fell his way. Yes, his Mercedes certainly started the year as the dominant package, but it’s what he did with it that was so impressive.

Antonelli still had to beat a much more experienced team mate in Russell. He had to out-qualify, out-race and overall outperform someone who went toe-to-toe with Hamilton and came out on top. He was placed in so many situations where it took more than just raw speed to win. It took good decision making. It took exceptional race craft. It took the kind of calm under pressure that simply can’t be taught.

In the same way that when Mercedes dominated the mid-teens, or Verstappen crushed the competition in the 2023 season, you could separate the driver’s accomplishment from the superior machinery. When you did that this season, some of Antonelli’s performances were simply sublime.

And Antonelli hasn’t had the best car all season. As the competition got better – got closer – he kept his cool and kept executing at a level that you’d expect from someone far his senior in both age and experience.

When you saw Hamilton’s early performances, when you saw Verstappen’s, you thought you were watching something special. And you were right. They went on to be the two most dominant drivers of their day. You get that same feeling watching Antonelli. It made the visuals from that Mexico podium all the more prophetic.

Pull up a chair. We’re witnessing greatness.

title: Piastri on his tough 2026 and why it could make him stronger
excerpt:
By his own admission, 2026 has been tough for Oscar Piastri. The season began with a DNS in front of his home crowd in Australia, was swiftly followed by another in China, and has brought with it significant challenges – particularly the task of getting to grips with McLaren’s MCL40.

While he currently sits a place behind team mate Lando Norris in the Drivers’ Championship, he is 94 points away from the Briton in seventh. Norris also has three wins this year, the most recent of which came last weekend in Sao Paulo, while Piastri has only been on the podium twice – and those were in rounds three and four of the campaign.

It’s a significant contrast to 2025 when the 25-year-old was embroiled in an intense three-way fight for the title that went all the way to the last race of the season, before Norris eventually triumphed and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen settled for second.

But the results do not tell the whole story of Piastri’s 2026 so far. While the change of regulations brought about an obvious reset in the pecking order – with Mercedes emerging as the class of the field to displace McLaren, who had won the last two Constructors’ Championships – there has also been a significant technical challenge for the Australian to overcome. It’s an exercise that has been far from straight forward.

‘It’s been tougher than I expected’

“It's been tough, definitely been tough,” Piastri admits to me as we catch up ahead of the United States Grand Prix in Austin. At this point he’s just come off a P5 result in Singapore and it looks like things are coming together again after a difficult first half of the year.

At the heart of his difficulties have been his struggles to adapt his natural driving style to the demands of McLaren’s MCL40 car. As mentioned by Team Principal Andrea Stella, Piastri has been unable to drive through “pure instinct” in certain conditions.

“As a team, we've not been as competitive as we would have wanted obviously and, I think for me, personally it's been tougher than I expected with trying to get to grips with the car,” the Australian continues.

“Obviously as a sport it's been a very demanding year in terms of getting used to the power units as well. It's definitely thrown in a lot of challenges, and I feel like I've had to change a lot of things in how I drive, or certainly tweak things.

“But I feel I'm making some progress now in the second half of this year, so yeah, just trying to continue that.”

McLaren’s drivers have both said at various points that the MCL40 is a difficult beast to tame, and it takes a lot to extract its full potential. But, for Piastri, that’s been coupled with having to retrain the driving instincts that have come so naturally to him over the last few years.

It’s no easy feat and, as any athlete will testify, when you’re having to think that intensely about the adjustments you need to make then it becomes increasingly hard to find your optimum performance level.

Piastri and management team mutually terminate agreement

“The biggest thing has probably been the general driving style you have, or that you need, is quite different for this year's car compared to previous years,” the 25-year-old explains.

“Even in previous years there's been an element of adaptation and learning for that – sure – but I think [it’s been a] combination of a few different things this year.

“Obviously, the cars are smaller, the tyres are quite different. It means you really have to drive the car on the edge all of the time – certainly our car, I don't know what others think of it.

“That's been quite different. You're always driving on the edge to an extent, but this year it's really always taking you beyond the edge of trying to salvage things.

“So, it's felt quite different to previous [cars] and even a lot of the previous cars I've driven in general. That's been quite an adaptation process and learning to trust the car and retrain what feels like the limit is never an easy thing to try and adapt. But hopefully I’m making progress.”

Without doubt Piastri is making that progress he is hoping for. Over the Singapore Grand Prix weekend, McLaren CEO Zak Brown said as much as he acknowledged the Australian was back to the driver he knew.

“He’s feeling more confident and on top of things,” Brown explained in the Team Principals’ Press Conference. “I like where both our drivers are now.”

While Piastri would perhaps rather have had another season fighting for titles, as he was in 2025, he does acknowledge that, in the long term, it might be a positive for him to have gone through the technical challenges that have been thrown at him this year.

“I think so,” he responds when I propose that line of thought. “You know, even some of the challenges from last year, they weren't completely dissimilar to what I've got this year, and I feel like I've definitely made a lot of progress on that in general.

“These last few races are definitely going to be another challenge in terms of testing where I'm at, in terms of developing those skills. Having that challenge has been tough, obviously, but getting through it, and then continuing to work on it, [is] ultimately going to be rewarding and [will] hopefully set me up for whatever car we get [in future].”

‘It's been good to see everybody pulling together’

Despite the way 2026 has panned out, with McLaren playing catch up following their back-to-back championship-winning years, the atmosphere within the squad is still positive.

Of course, part of the reason they began this season on the back foot was because last year’s drivers’ title went right down to the wire in the Abu Dhabi finale – Red Bull, after all, found themselves in the exact same position.

But as the year has gone on the team have found gains through development, one of their key strengths over the last few seasons, and Piastri insists they are as determined as ever to return to the top.

“It's been good to see everybody pulling together and this year has definitely been more challenging for sure,” says Piastri as I ask about the atmosphere within the squad. “I think everyone is still very determined to get back to where we know we can be.

Stella reveals how McLaren triumphed at Interlagos

“The competition [to Mercedes] is definitely going to step up in terms of, not just the competitiveness they have, but the continued development and stuff like that. They're raising the bar as well.

“I feel like we've set the bar pretty high in the last couple of years and that's the beauty of F1 – everyone is always pushing the boundaries further and further.

“I think we're on our way back there, development and upgrades have always been a strong point for us, and hopefully we can just keep pushing.”

There’s also plenty to be said about a team growing stronger in times of adversity, which Piastri is also seeing first hand. McLaren have, after all, roared back from difficult situations before.

“Definitely between myself, and the pretty close and intimate engineering team around me, we've learned a lot about each other and how we get the most out of ourselves [as well as] how we get more out of ourselves,” he explains. “So that's been a good process to go through for sure.”

‘I've always tried to remove results from what success looks like’

As is so often said in the intense world of F1, you live and die by the stopwatch. So, given Piastri and McLaren have not been able to deliver the results they both might have wanted, what has brought the Australian joy this year?

“I think trying to make progress,” he answers. “I've always tried to remove results from what success looks like.

“Of course, results do help. But especially when you're not in a position to win races, or whether it be because of the car or the kind of struggles I've had this year, sometimes a win and a successful weekend looks like improvement rather than perfection, is what I would say.

“That's brought me joy, for sure. There's been some very strong weekends this year that I've been really happy with. [I’m] just trying to work through those things.”

And what also comes as an additional challenge for drivers, when things aren’t going as well as hoped, is wrapping up your self-worth and identity entirely in F1 and what you do on the track.

“I mean, it is definitely a challenge because we spend so much time working at races and stuff like that,” Piastri adds. “It's definitely a challenge to be able to switch off from that.

“But I think outside of the track, I still enjoy the same things I always have – being able to spend time with my girlfriend, being able to have a few hours, a few days to kind of decompress, watch TV, play my simulator, play video games, whatever it might be. They're the same things that bring me joy, so yeah, that side of things hasn't changed.”

All you need to know about Oscar Piastri

Piastri has always been praised for that level-headed approach. It’s proved beneficial when fighting for titles, and it will absolutely be beneficial now as he seeks to turn around his fortunes.

Of course, what also helps is the strong sense of belief he has that McLaren will be back fighting for championships in the very near future.

“I certainly hope so,” he says. “I think it's been intriguing this year to see how things have ebbed and flowed.

“Everyone's kind of had their strong moments in terms of the top four teams. So yeah, we're pushing very hard to get back to that of course. Like I said, the teams around us have definitely raised the bar, but I know that we can raise it even higher.”

title: Why are F1 drivers obsessed with padel?
excerpt:
Padel has become an increasingly popular sport among Formula 1 drivers, with Fernando Alonso and George Russell teaming up on the court, while Pierre Gasly has even invested in his own team. Now Aston Martin have taken that connection a step further with the launch of a new collection of padel rackets.

Padel has found a growing following within the paddock. But what exactly is the sport, and why have so many F1 drivers taken to it?

Aston Martin bring F1 to the padel court

Ahead of the 2026 United States Grand Prix,Aston Martin announced a collaboration with racket sports brand Padeltek, becoming the first F1 team to formally partner with a company specialising in padel and pickleball.

The collection features three padel rackets and accompanying cover bags, with pickleball equipment set to follow in 2027. To celebrate the launch, Aston Martin hosted an event in Austin, where Jenson Button, Jessica Hawkins, Jak Crawford and Pedro de la Rosa took to the court.

For Matt Chapman, Aston Martin's Head of Licensing and Merchandise, the sport's popularity within the paddock presented an opportunity to explore a new area for the team.

"Padel was a particularly interesting opportunity given its incredible growth and the natural connection it has developed with the Formula 1 paddock," Chapman told F1.com.

"We've seen how popular the sport has become among drivers and teams, but the appeal goes much further than that. It has a global and diverse community, which presents an exciting opportunity for us to connect with new audiences and explore a different side of our brand."

However, Chapman explained that the team wanted to ensure the collaboration went beyond simply adding its branding to existing equipment.

"Authenticity was really important to us from the outset. We wanted to create something that went beyond simply putting our name on a product, ensuring the collection genuinely reflected both our identity and the demands of the sport.

"Working with Padeltek allowed us to bring together their expertise in padel equipment, with our own design. We wanted the collection to feel unmistakably Aston Martin, while ensuring the products were designed to perform on court. Striking that balance between design, functionality and performance was key."

Aston Martin's Chief Marketing Officer, Rob Bloom, believes the competitive similarities between Formula 1 and padel have contributed to the sport's popularity.

"There's a natural crossover between the two sports, particularly when you consider the competitive mindset and the importance of quick thinking, precision and reaction times," Bloom told F1.com.

"Padel has become a sport that has brought people together, whether that's drivers, team members or fans, and it's become a great way for the paddock to connect away from the intensity of a race weekend."

What is padel, and why do F1 drivers love it?

Combining elements of tennis and squash, padel is typically played in doubles on an enclosed court surrounded by glass walls and fencing.

The scoring system is similar to tennis, but players serve underarm, use solid rackets and can return shots after the ball rebounds off the surrounding walls. The fast-paced rallies demand quick reactions, communication and teamwork, qualities that also play an important role in Formula 1.

According to Mike Dale, Editor of The Padel Paper, its accessibility is a major part of the appeal, particularly for professional athletes.

"Padel has indeed become really popular with current and ex-sportsmen and women. The sport is obviously very trendy and quite a lot of the emerging clubs are quite high-end, so the environment is attractive to people from the equally glamorous F1 world," he told F1.com.

"But the biggest reason is that padel is very easy to become quite good at quite quickly, particularly if you've got a baseline of athleticism, sporting ability and hand-eye coordination. And that feeling of being 'good' quite quickly is very addictive!"

The social element is another attraction for drivers, with Lando Norris, Oscar Piastri, Carlos Sainz, and Charles Leclerc among those regularly enjoying matches away from the track.

Ahead of the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix, Norris and Gabriel Bortoleto were spotted enjoying a game, while Alex Albon revealed that drivers had even established a group chat to organise late-night matches during the race weekend.

Despite taking place away from the pressures of a Grand Prix weekend, their competitive instincts remain.

Fernando Alonso has played padel for well over a decade, and during the 2023 Mexico City Grand Prix weekend revealed that he and Russell had enjoyed an unbeaten record together.

"I was [impressed by Russell]. I've been playing padel for, 12 or 15 years," Alonso said.

"But I think George is quite new to it and he was strong. And we are unbeatable at the moment! We play once and it's 100% dominant wins!"

Russell, meanwhile, explained that padel had become a welcome hobby during the latter stages of the season.

"Team mates on the padel court, 100% record against our competitors. It's always nice to do that as a sport, I've been getting into it a little bit as this year has progressed, and especially this time of the season, you spend a lot of time away, so it's nice to have a hobby on the side."

Piastri has also admitted that the drivers take their matches rather seriously.

"We take it far too seriously, yes. But it's very good fun and a good way of, you know, just keeping yourself awake."

Gasly takes his passion for padel further

While many drivers enjoy padel recreationally, Pierre Gasly has become involved in the sport as a team owner.

The Alpine driver is an investor in 10Padel, a team competing in the Hexagon Cup, an international padel competition which has attracted several high-profile investors.

"Padel is something I really enjoy in my daily life, and I believe it's a sport with incredible business potential," Gasly told Reuters in February 2026. "I'm happy to be a part of its growth through my team."

For Gasly, exploring interests outside Formula 1 is an important part of his life.

"Formula 1 opens many opportunities. While I wake up thinking about F1 and fall asleep thinking about it, there's more to life. I want to discover other things and mix them with my passions," he explained.

Could Formula 1 help padel reach new audiences?

With drivers regularly sharing their enthusiasm for padel and Aston Martin introducing its own equipment collection, the relationship between the two sports continues to develop.

For Aston Martin's Bloom, the partnership offers an opportunity to engage with fans beyond the traditional motorsport environment.

"Formula 1 has an incredibly diverse fanbase, and for Aston Martin, it's about finding authentic ways to meet fans on their terms – that means in their communities beyond motorsport. Padel is a great example of that.

"Collaborations like this allow fans to engage with the team through something they enjoy themselves, creating a connection that extends beyond the racetrack. Ultimately, we want to be part of the conversations and communities that matter to our fans, wherever their interests lie."

Dale similarly believes that partnerships involving F1 teams and drivers could help introduce padel to new audiences.

"These F1 and padel partnerships help raise padel's profile even more. There's a massive investor buzz around padel, with new clubs, tech, equipment and apparel being launched on a daily basis."

He also highlighted the influence of high-profile figures, including football legends David Beckham, Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, in attracting potential players.

"When people see these celebrities on their social timelines holding a racket and smiling, it raises public awareness and curiosity about the game. It also makes it aspirational. 'If Beckham or Lando's doing it, I want to try it too!'"

Padel has also made appearances at Grand Prix venues, with courts installed at Silverstone in recent years and an area dedicated to the sport at the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

For fans tempted to follow their favourite drivers onto the court, Dale believes the ease of picking up the game is one of its greatest strengths.

"Almost anyone can go on court and have enjoyable rallies straight away – friends, families, all ages and abilities. You quite quickly get that magic feeling of 'I can do this!', which then equally quickly becomes, 'I'm good at this!' and that's very addictive."

With drivers competing against each other away from the track and teams beginning to get involved, padel is becoming an increasingly familiar part of life in the F1 paddock. And judging by the enthusiasm of those already playing, the competition is unlikely to remain confined to the circuit.

title: Toto Wolff's journey from Williams to nine F1 titles
excerpt:
After guiding Mercedes to a ninth Constructors' Championship, Toto Wolff has drawn level with Sir Frank Williams in the history books. Here is how the Austrian became one of Formula 1's most successful team bosses.

When Mercedes secured their ninth Constructors' Championship at the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix, it marked another significant milestone in the career of Team Principal Toto Wolff.

The result saw the Silver Arrows draw level with Williams on nine teams' titles, placing them behind only Ferrari and McLaren in Formula 1 history. For Wolff, the achievement carried particular significance given his beginnings in the sport.

Before overseeing Mercedes' record-breaking run of eight consecutive Constructors' Championships, the Austrian had made his first steps into Formula 1 management at Williams, working alongside the team's legendary founder, Sir Frank Williams.

Now, more than a decade after joining Mercedes, Wolff has matched Frank's tally of nine Constructors' titles, having guided the Brackley-based outfit back to the top following four seasons without championship success.

But how did a former racing driver and businessman become one of Formula 1's most successful team bosses?

A racing driver turned businessman

Born in Vienna in 1972, Wolff's motorsport career began behind the wheel rather than on the pit wall. After developing an interest in racing as a teenager, he competed in Austrian Formula Ford and claimed a class victory at the 1994 Nürburgring 24 Hours.

His racing career also included an appearance in the FIA GT Championship in 2004, although by this point, Wolff had already begun establishing himself in the business world, realising his talents lay beyond the cockpit.

He founded investment firms Marchfifteen in 1998 and Marchsixteen in 2004, with interests spanning technology and industrial businesses, while maintaining his connections to motorsport.

Those interests included HWA AG, the company responsible for Mercedes-Benz's DTM and Formula 3 programmes, providing Wolff with experience of the commercial and competitive sides of racing before entering Formula 1 management.

Finding his feet at Williams

Wolff's involvement in Formula 1 began in 2009 when he invested in Williams, a team already established as one of the most successful in the sport's history.

Founded by Sir Frank Williams and Sir Patrick Head, the outfit had won nine Constructors' Championships between 1980 and 1997, enjoying success with drivers including Nigel Mansell, Alain Prost, Damon Hill and Jacques Villeneuve.

Although Williams were no longer regularly challenging for titles when Wolff arrived, the Austrian developed a close relationship with Frank, eventually becoming the team's Executive Director in 2012.

Reflecting on their relationship in a 2020 interview with F1.com, Wolff recalled the moment they first met.

"Frank Williams is an incredible person, with an aura and charisma that very few people in Formula 1 possess. I was lucky enough to meet him personally in 2009, and I'll never forget the first thing he said to me: 'I heard you can help me repay my mortgage!'"

Wolff's time at Williams would prove relatively brief, however, as another opportunity emerged in 2013.

A new chapter with Mercedes

In February 2013, Wolff joined Mercedes as Managing Partner, acquiring a 30% stake in the Formula 1 operation and taking on wider responsibilities for the manufacturer's motorsport activities. The move placed him alongside three-time World Champion Niki Lauda and Team Principal Ross Brawn as Mercedes continued building towards the front of the grid.

Wolff's first season coincided with Lewis Hamilton arriving at Mercedes to join Nico Rosberg, beginning one of the most successful partnerships in the sport's history.

Mercedes secured three victories during the 2013 campaign, with Rosberg winning in Monaco and Great Britain before Hamilton took victory in Hungary. The team eventually finished second in the Constructors' Championship behind Red Bull.

However, the introduction of new turbo-hybrid power unit regulations in 2014 would transform the competitive order.

Mercedes won 16 of the season's 19 Grands Prix, while Hamilton secured his second Drivers' Championship after a season-long battle with Rosberg. The result also delivered the team's first Constructors' title.

It was the beginning of an unprecedented period of success.

Eight consecutive championships

Mercedes' dominance continued throughout the following seasons, as Wolff oversaw a team that established a new benchmark for consistency in Formula 1.

Hamilton added further Drivers' Championships in 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2020, while Rosberg defeated his childhood friend and team mate to claim the 2016 crown. And while despite the intense rivalry between their drivers, Mercedes maintained their position at the front, navigating regulation changes and challenges from Ferrari and Red Bull.

By 2021, the Silver Arrows had won eight consecutive Constructors' Championships, a record unmatched by any other Formula 1 team.

Although Hamilton narrowly missed out on an eighth Drivers' title to Max Verstappen that season, Mercedes secured another teams' crown, extending their extraordinary run of success.

A ninth title and a place alongside Frank Williams

Mercedes' remarkable winning streak ended in 2022, as the introduction of new ground effect regulations changed the competitive landscape and left the team struggling to match their rivals.

For Wolff, it marked the beginning of a challenging period, with Mercedes managing just five Grand Prix victories across the following four seasons. Despite the setbacks, the Austrian remained at the helm, overseeing changes to the team's driver line-up and preparations for another major regulation overhaul in 2026.

Hamilton's departure for Ferrari at the end of 2024 also marked the conclusion of one of Formula 1's most successful driver-team partnerships, with Wolff choosing to promote young Italian Kimi Antonelli alongside George Russell.

"I made up my mind five minutes after Lewis Hamilton told me that he's going to Ferrari," said Wolff following Antonelli's announcement in August 2024.

"That is the line-up with these two [Russell and Antonelli] that I always wanted, bearing in mind the fast-tracking that we did with Kimi and everything related there too, but that was immediately what I wanted to do."

The decision represented a significant show of faith in the then 18-year-old, who had progressed through Mercedes' junior programme before making his Formula 1 debut in 2025.

“Wolff's decision was vindicated in 2026, with Antonelli securing his maiden Drivers' Championship at the Mexico City Grand Prix, becoming the youngest World Champion in F1 history at just 20 years old.”

Mercedes' resurgence was completed at the following round in Sao Paulo, where Russell and Antonelli's fourth and fifth-place finishes secured the team's ninth Constructors' Championship, ending a four-year wait for another title.

The achievement marked Mercedes' ninth Constructors' Championship, their first since 2021, and brought Wolff level with Sir Frank Williams, whose nine titles had been won across the 1980s and 1990s.

Speaking to Sky Sports following the race, Wolff reflected on the significance of matching the man who had helped him establish his career in Formula 1.

"Obviously, Frank is such an unbelievable icon of the sport, and to be tied on constructors' championships, I never thought that was ever possible.

"I had a close relationship with Frank, and to be there, it's amazing. I can't believe it."

title: Oscar Piastri makes admission about recent F1 form: 'I definitely have not been...'
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has conceded he has not been "in a state of flow" for most of the F1 season as he struggles to get comfortable with the championship's new-generation cars.

Piastri has gone winless through the opening 20 grands prix, whilst Lando Norris has taken three victories. His McLaren team-mate's latest success in São Paulo, where the Australian finished sixth, extended the gap between them to 94 points.

It marks a significant change from last year's title challenge, when Piastri won seven races and established a 34-point advantage over Norris before slipping behind both the Briton and Max Verstappen, finishing 13 points short of the championship.

Having thrived in the previous ground-effect machinery, he explained that adapting to the new power units initially masked difficulties with the handling of his MCL40.

"It's been challenging for sure," Piastri told the Up To Speed podcast when addressing his season. "I think there's probably been two challenges this year.

"The power units, definitely. That was a massive reset and unlearning and rewiring a lot of things you've learned since you were a kid.

"But I think once we got our heads around that, then actually understanding the behaviour of the cars as well is quite different.

"So, I felt like at the beginning of the year, actually, we were doing a really good job of getting on top of some of the quirks, let's say, of how you needed to drive to get lap time from the power unit and use your battery efficiently and stuff.

"And then once the rules changed a little bit and it became a little bit easier, that kind of got put on the side and actually went back to the normal things you would look out for in terms of the way the car behaves and things like that.

"It was once we put all the power unit stuff to the side and we focused a bit more on what the car was actually doing that there was there was a few things that weren't quite as nice as I would have liked. And it's been tough this year to get on top of those as well."

[Article continues below]

Piastri missing 'state of flow'

Piastri's podiums in Japan and Miami remain his only top-three grand prix finishes this season, with the 25-year-old describing how the demands of the latest cars have prevented driving from feeling instinctive.

"You ask any racing driver, or probably any athlete... When they're performing at their best, and everything comes easily, you're not thinking about what you're doing," Piastri added.

"Like you're just in this state of flow, basically. And I definitely have not been in a state of flow for most of this year.

"Even the cars themselves, especially compared to the previous cars we've driven, [are] a quite different beast. So, that's taken quite a bit of getting used to, for sure.

"And again, I've had to learn how to drive in pretty different ways. Also, racing people is a bit different now that there's no more DRS; everything's with the battery. So, you've got to spread your energy and your thought process out over more areas now, which certainly doesn't help things either."

title: Formula E twelfth team finally official as Fusion arrival confirmed
excerpt:
Fusion Formula E has been confirmed as the 12th team on the grid for the ABB FIA Formula E World Championship, joining the series ahead of its new Gen4 era in 2027.

The British-based squad will field two Porsche 975 RSE cars as part of a 24-car grid, with the new generation of machinery marking what the championship is billing as its biggest technical leap yet.

Phil Charles has been appointed team principal, with Chris Bluett taking on the role of Sporting Director.

The new outfit is part of the wider Fusion Racing Group, which has been expanding its international motorsport portfolio, and this marks the group's first entry into FIA World Championship competition.

Charles and Bluett have been recruiting engineers, mechanics and operational staff from across Formula E and the broader motorsport industry as they build the team from scratch.

Chiko Nanji, group executive vice chairman of Fusion Racing Group, said Formula E offered the right platform for the group's ambitions.

title: Mercedes predict significant loss for start of new F1 season
excerpt:
F1 underwent a considerable regulations overhaul for the 2026 season, and further changes are coming. Mercedes technical director James Allison has shared his thoughts.

Mercedes technical director James Allison expects F1 cars to lose a significant amount of downforce at the start of the 2027 season as the FIA revises the chassis and aerodynamic rules introduced this year.

The changes include a shallower rear wing and tighter restrictions on the design of the front of the floor.

The FIA has also outlawed the small wings teams have used around the exhaust to generate extra downforce at the rear of the car.

When host Anthony Davidson suggested on Mercedes' Nu Silver Arrows Podcast that the cars would lose a bit of downforce, Allison gave a stronger assessment.

"I think more than a bit," Allison explained. "They've had a good go at trying to pull the downforce back to the start of the 2026 era.

"And it will be interesting to see whether the teams lie down and take that or whether we recover it all or not. And the PUs, the changes there are not as small as maybe they're advertised."

[Article continues below]

'Far more than a tweak...'

The revised hybrid rules will shift the nominal split between combustion and electric power from 53:47 to 58:42 in 2027, with a further move to 60:40 planned for 2028.

Next season's rules raise the fuel energy flow limit by five per cent and cap standard electrical deployment at 300 kW. The FIA wants drivers to be able to spend more of a qualifying lap at full throttle.

Asked about the scale of the power unit changes, Allison replied, "[It is] far more than a tweak. It's quite a big change."

Mercedes secured their first title double since 2020 when they clinched the constructors' championship in São Paulo with three rounds to spare, a week after Kimi Antonelli won the drivers' title in Mexico.

Davidson put it to Allison that rivals had closed in on Mercedes, estimating the team's early-season advantage at eight and a half tenths of a second.

"Oh, I don't think you allow others to catch," he responded. "You can put whatever narrative you like on it, but I think that we started the season super duper strong and we did so for several reasons.

"I think we were better prepared than many others. I think we had a better handle on the energy management at the start of the year."

title: Red Bull make surprisingly-priced purchase from Ford to kick off new F1 venture - On This Day
excerpt:
22 years ago today, Ford confirmed Red Bull had purchased the Jaguar Racing F1 team for just $1. Two decades later, the two companies would join forces...

On 15 November 2004, Ford Motor Company confirmed it had sold Jaguar Racing to Red Bull, closing the book on a troubled factory project and opening the door to what would become one of Formula 1's most successful teams.

The American manufacturer simultaneously confirmed the divestment of engine builder Cosworth to Champ Car owners Kevin Kalkhoven and Gerald Forsythe, drawing a line under its wider involvement in grand prix racing.

No official transaction figure was ever published, but it was revealed Ford had sold the team for a nominal $1, on condition that Red Bull committed to funding operations and ploughing hundreds of millions of dollars — believed to be $400 million — into the project over the following seasons.

Ford had first signalled its intention to quit F1 in September 2004, after a strategic review concluded there was no longer a compelling business case for any of its brands to remain in the championship.

Ford group vice-president Richard Parry-Jones said at the time that the move marked "the passing of an era," adding: "After over 35 years in the sport, deciding to exit F1 was a very tough decision for us to make."

Jaguar's struggles were rooted in soaring costs and financial strain across Ford's core road car business, with restructuring and job losses at its Coventry manufacturing base coinciding with the team's decline on track.

Ford had concluded it could not match the roughly $200 million budgets of rivals such as Ferrari, Mercedes and BMW, making a backmarker campaign under a premium badge untenable.

[Article continues below]

A costly Ford failure

Jaguar technical director Gary Anderson later placed much of the blame on Ford's internal culture rather than a lack of resources.

"We had some very clever individuals from Ford working with us, but they were tied up by Ford's bureaucracy," Anderson said years later.

"This made it very difficult for them to express themselves and get on with it rather than protecting themselves from the people at Ford, who were themselves just looking after their pensions and being yes men to their superiors."

Parry-Jones struck a more conciliatory tone as the sale was finalised, praising the backing the team had received from its own staff. "I am really pleased that Red Bull has bought Jaguar Racing," he said.

"Since we announced our intention to sell our Formula 1 businesses back in September, we have had fantastic support from both the management and employees of Jaguar Racing."

For Red Bull founder Dietrich Mateschitz, the purchase of the Milton Keynes squad, originally built by Jackie Stewart before its sale to Ford in 2000, represented the logical next step after a decade of motorsport investment.

"There are things which, alongside their strategic fit and logicality, also give me personally a great deal of pleasure," Mateschitz said. "Our own Red Bull team in Formula 1 is definitely one of those." He called the takeover "a provisional summit of our 10-year involvement in motor sport."

Mateschitz did not stop there. Less than a year later, he signed an agreement with Paul Stoddart during the Belgian Grand Prix weekend in September 2005 to acquire the Minardi outfit outright, with official ownership transferring to Red Bull on 1 November 2005.

Stoddart made preserving the Faenza base and its workforce a condition of the sale, while Red Bull's motivation was rather different to the Jaguar deal: this purchase was intended primarily as a proving ground for its growing roster of junior drivers.

Minardi, the perennial Italian backmarker that had contested 643 grands prix without a win or a podium to its name, gave Red Bull a second chassis on the grid and a pipeline for its young talent.

That Faenza entry has since undergone several transformations. It became Scuderia Toro Rosso for 2006, an Italian rendering of the Red Bull name chosen to honour the team's roots, before being rebranded Scuderia AlphaTauri ahead of 2020 to promote Red Bull's fashion and apparel label on the global stage.

Ahead of the 2024 season, the team adopted its current identity as Racing Bulls, built around the RB chassis name to tie it more closely into the wider Red Bull corporate structure alongside commercial partners Visa and Cash App.

[Article continues below]

From Jaguar's wreckage to a six-time champion

Twenty-two years on, that provisional summit has become one of the defining success stories in modern F1.

Red Bull has gone on to win six constructors' championships and 136 of its 913 race entries, climbing from the back of the Jaguar grid to become a dominant force through the Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen eras alike.

Ford's own return to the paddock has come full circle too. The manufacturer re-entered F1 in 2026 as technical partner to Red Bull Powertrains, under a deal agreed back in 2023 running through at least 2030, supplying battery cell technology, electric motor design and control software for the new hybrid regulations.

Ford chief executive Jim Farley framed the comeback around the company's broader direction.

"Ford's return to Formula 1 with Red Bull Racing is all about where we are going as a company, increasingly electric, software-defined, modern vehicles and experiences," he said.

Ford Performance director Mark Rushbrook detailed the scope of that collaboration earlier this year.

"When we arrived, we said that Ford wanted to focus on the electric side. And that's where we've put our main focus," he said. "But beyond that, we've been able to contribute our expertise in controls and calibration to combine the combustion engine with electrification."

The results through 2026 have been strong if not spectacular. Red Bull sits third in the constructors' standings with 415 points and three wins after 20 rounds, behind Mercedes and Ferrari but ahead of McLaren, as the Milton Keynes-based squad continues building its in-house power unit project from scratch.

Rushbrook has stressed the value of real-world data as the partnership beds in.

"As much as we can see in our offline simulation, even using the driver in the simulator, getting their real feedback from the track is very important," he said.

title: Departing long-time Red Bull figure makes Max Verstappen declaration
excerpt:
Red Bull mechanic Ole Schack paid a heartfelt tribute to Max Verstappen as he prepared to leave the team after around two decades of service.

Schack called time on his Red Bull career after last weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos, with the mechanic keen to spend more time with his family.

The Dane has worked closely with Verstappen for years and used the occasion to reflect on what makes the four-time champion so special.

Speaking to De Telegraaf, Schack explained that the day-to-day nature of the job means the little details often go unnoticed.

"There are so many small things that make it special to work with him," said Schack.

"But it doesn't stand out any more, because it's just our daily life. I know his typical habits when he's in the car. But he's basically still the same guy as ten years ago. Always honest, just like how he talks to the media."

Schack did not hold back when drawing a comparison for the Dutchman, saying: "He's like Ronaldo and Messi, but in a Formula 1 car. Max just has that little bit extra that you can't teach someone."

Red Bull environment 'out of the ordinary'

Schack also reflected on the environment at Red Bull, which he has always found to be something out of the ordinary.

"Here they've always done things just a little bit differently. With our own Energy Station and that incredible season-opening party in Melbourne that kicks everything off."

Despite the growth, Schack insisted the team has held on to its identity.

"We've become more mature, but we still play the loudest music in the pit lane," he added. "Even guys who've come over from other teams say the atmosphere here is very different. It's in our blood."

title: Sergio Perez shares 'key' ingredient in clear demand over Cadillac team-mate

Perez shares 'all he needs' from team-mate

title: Lewis Hamilton matches F1 history after Lance Stroll achieves career first
excerpt:
Six years ago today, Lewis Hamilton equalled Michael Schumacher's record of seven F1 drivers' championships after Lance Stroll started from pole at the 2020 Turkish Grand Prix.

15 November 2:00PM

The story of 15 November 2020 remains one of Formula 1's most remarkable afternoons.

Six years ago to this day, Lewis Hamilton clinched his seventh F1 drivers' championship in treacherous conditions at Istanbul Park, equalling Michael Schumacher's long-standing record, on the very day Lance Stroll started from pole position for the first time in his F1 career.

The Turkish Grand Prix had been added to the championship's pandemic-reshuffled calendar almost as one of many stand-ins, but it produced one of the defining days in the sport's history.

Stroll topped a chaotic qualifying session on a newly resurfaced, low-grip circuit made worse by rain, putting his Racing Point on pole ahead of Max Verstappen and team-mate Sergio Perez. Hamilton could only manage sixth for Mercedes, over four seconds off Stroll's pace.

Come race day, Stroll converted pole into a lead he held for 32 laps. But his car suffered a loss of pace that baffled him in the immediate aftermath.

"It was kind of the right thing to do but then the next set grained again, and we just went further back, so it's really hard to understand what happened," the Canadian said.

Racing Point later established the cause: a broken strake had lodged beneath the front wing, costing Stroll crucial front downforce. He eventually finished ninth.

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lance Stroll

Canadian

18

Hamilton's gamble on worn rubber

As others pitted for fresh intermediates, Hamilton did the opposite, running his tyres down to near-slicks and refusing to change them. The decision, counterintuitive on a drying but still damp track, proved decisive: worn intermediates gripped better than cold, grooved replacements prone to severe graining.

Hamilton later explained the thinking behind staying out.

"I was thinking about moments when it went wrong before, like China 2007 when I lost the championship on worn tyres in the pit lane," he said, reflecting on his title-deciding retirement 13 years earlier. "All these things I've learned along the way, I was able to apply today."

He crossed the line to win by over 31 seconds from Perez, who claimed his first podium of the season after a last-lap pass on Charles Leclerc, with Sebastian Vettel completing the podium in third, his only rostrum of the 2020 campaign.

Vettel admitted the podium came as something of a surprise. "It was quite intense, quite long, but good fun," the German said.

"Obviously it was very intense in the last lap and yeah, a bit of a surprise to snatch the podium in the end but certainly very happy."

Perez, for his part, revealed just how close his tyres had come to failure. "I told my team on the radio, 'I think one more lap on those tyres, I think they would have exploded,'" he said. "The vibrations were extremely bad towards the end, but I think it also made our race."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

A seventh crown for Hamilton

The win sealed Hamilton's seventh F1 drivers' title with three rounds still to run, Valtteri Bottas having entered the weekend as the only other driver mathematically in contention, 85 points behind.

Hamilton, visibly emotional afterwards, struggled to process the achievement.

"I'm definitely a bit lost for words," he said. "I dreamed of this as a kid. This is way, way beyond our dreams."

Over the radio moments after crossing the line, he had already found the words he wanted the world to hear. "That's for all the kids out there who dream the impossible. You can do it too, man! I believe in you guys!"

Team principal Toto Wolff framed the win as proof of Hamilton's composure under pressure. "It shows how he's capable of coping with the situation that went against him at the beginning," Wolff said. "He was the only one who kept it on the road; that is the difference today."

Asked later about matching Schumacher's benchmark, Hamilton reflected on how distant the number seven had once seemed.

"I remember watching Michael winning the championships, and just to get one, or two, or three, it's so hard to get," he said. "Seven is just unimaginable."

title: Former Liberty Media boss makes striking prediction for F1 future
excerpt:
Former Liberty Media chief executive Greg Maffei has predicted that Formula 1 could disappear from the stock market within the next two years, citing the sport's rapid commercial growth since the American company's 2017 takeover.

Liberty Media acquired F1 from a CVC Capital Partners-led consortium in a deal worth around $8 billion. Since then, the sport's commercial value has soared, with the Formula One Group, which now also includes MotoGP, carrying a market value of close to $28 billion.

F1's financial growth has been reflected in its annual results. The sport generated $3.411 billion in revenue for the full 2024 financial year, up from $3.222 billion in 2023.

That growth continued into 2025, with Liberty Media reporting full-year F1 revenue of $3.9 billion, a 14 per cent year-on-year increase.

Analysts have pointed to several factors behind F1's commercial expansion under Liberty Media, including the introduction of the cost cap in 2021, expansion into new US markets, growing digital reach through Netflix's Drive to Survive, and the enlargement of the calendar to 24 races.

The docuseries has also been credited with broadening F1's audience, helping push the sport's female fan share to roughly 40 per cent globally, with women making up around half of its Gen Z following.

Apple's theatrical film F1, directed by Joseph Kosinski, added a further boost this year, surpassing $600 million in worldwide box office and contributing to increased US live viewership and F1 TV signups.

The growth has also pushed up the value of individual teams. By late 2025, the average valuation of an active F1 team had risen to $3.6 billion, an 89 per cent increase compared with 2023 estimates, with every team now valued at no less than $1.5 billion.

Ferrari was rated as the most valuable team at $6.5 billion, closely followed by Mercedes at around $6 billion after a private minority equity transaction.

Liberty Media added MotoGP to its portfolio in 2025, buying it from Dorna Sports in a deal worth an estimated €4.3 billion in enterprise value, leaving the American company well placed to cash in on the growth of its motorsport holdings.

However, Maffei does not see that rate of growth continuing, making a remarkable claim when speaking at Sportico's Invest New York 2026 conference.

When asked whether Formula 1 will still be on the stock market two years from now, he replied: "I'll say F1 is gone."

[Article continues below]

Why does Maffei think that?

Liberty announced recently that John Malone would step down as chairman emeritus. His voting power has also fallen from 48 per cent to three per cent after he exchanged shares carrying enhanced voting rights for shares with limited or no voting rights.

Any offer for Liberty Media would now be a matter for its board. Maffei said directors would have a fiduciary duty to consider what was in shareholders' best interests if a bid came in.

Maffei expects Formula 1 to keep growing, though at a much slower pace. Under Liberty, the series has expanded its calendar, increased its roster of global sponsors to 10 and staged more events in lucrative markets such as the United States and the Middle East.

In Maffei's view, there is now less scope to drive growth through those same measures.

"The easy money’s been made," he said. "The EBITDA [earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation] is up 3x in eight or nine years.

"It's not going to go up 3x again in the next eight or nine years."

title: Charles Leclerc highlights Lewis Hamilton 'sensitivity' in reflection on Ferrari team-mate
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has pinpointed what Lewis Hamilton is "sensitive to" as one of the biggest things he has learned from having the seven-time F1 drivers' champion as his team-mate.

The Ferrari drivers have endured a fraught relationship in recent weeks, but Leclerc was keen to underline how valuable he has found having a driver of Hamilton's experience and stature on the other side of the Italian team's garage.

The Monegasque driver has twice seen first-hand how F1 champions operate, having been alongside Sebastian Vettel at the Scuderia in 2019 and 2020 as well.

Leclerc has never been the more seasoned driver in a line-up across his F1 career, but seems perfectly content to continue absorbing as much as he can from Hamilton.

"Having Lewis as a team-mate, you always learn a massive amount, starting from inside the garage and in the meeting rooms, to understand how he works, what his priorities are, and what he's sensitive to," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

"I think from one driver to the other, it always differs: the sensitivities of a driver to one thing or the other. And then on track, it's obvious that, in terms of driving style, you always look at the other side of the garage to try and improve in the best possible way. So, for me, it's all around."

[Article continues below]

Leclerc' human side point

George Russell, who was sitting alongside Hamilton and Leclerc, shared a more human element of his relationship with his compatriot, having been team-mates at Mercedes for three campaigns from 2022 to 2024.

"Yes, a lot from Lewis, obviously. I joined [him] earlier in my career," he added. "Charles has pretty much summed it up for all the racing stuff.

"We've learned a lot about movies since spending time with Lewis, because he's quite into his movies and always shocked that I've not seen probably one per cent of what he's watched.

title: Lola and Mahindra reveal Formula E liveries as Gen4 testing awaits

title: Former F1 drivers take on staggering five-way Red Bull challenge
excerpt:
Two former Formula 1 drivers have lined up against a MotoGP legend, a rallycross champion, a snowmobile racer and a Pro 4 Truck driver in the first-ever Red Bull Ultimate Winter Race, held on a frozen lake in Eagle River, Wisconsin.

Patrick Friesacher, who drove for Minardi in the first half of the 2005 season and has since become a regular show-run driver for Red Bull Racing, took the wheel of the iconic RB7 for the five-way contest.

He was joined on the grid by Scott Speed, Red Bull's first American F1 driver who raced for Scuderia Toro Rosso in 2006 and part of 2007 before moving into rallycross and stock car racing.

Completing the line-up were MotoGP legend Dani Pedrosa, snowmobile racer Gunnar Sterne and Pro 4 Truck champion Andrew Carlson, all competing in temperatures of -17°C across 107 acres of ice.

Organisers designed unique sections into the course to balance the wildly different machinery, including shorter inside lines for vehicles less suited to winter conditions and longer outside routes for those built for the ice.

Pedrosa made the most of his MotoGP bike, fitted with custom spiked wheels, using his cornering ability and acceleration to take the chequered flag.

Friesacher's RB7 came home second despite being pushed well outside its natural habitat, with the snowmobile completing the podium on home conditions.

Friesacher revealed the lengths the team went to in order to make the Formula 1 car usable on ice, speaking after the event.

"Given it was -17 degrees Celsius, we made some modifications to the tyres and ride height. I would use longer spikes like Dani next time!

"It was tricky; sometimes you went into the corner too quickly, experienced understeer and had no traction, so you really need to be able to adapt to make those fine adjustments.

"Everything about Ultimate Winter Race, from the unique course to getting to compete alongside these great drivers, made it a special experience."

title: Fernando Alonso reveals major Honda F1 move after 'hard lessons'
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has said that Honda is developing a "completely new project" for 2027 after its poor first season back in F1.

The expectations for Aston Martin-Honda were high coming into 2026, with the first Adrian Newey-designed chassis, but problems on both the chassis and power unit side have wrecked the season.

The best result has been Alonso's eighth place in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia with eighth place, with Lance Stroll yet to get on the points board.
